bundles.tagline: A log summariser for the command line
bundles.desc: {brand} reads plain text log files and prints a short summary of what is in them.
bundles.overview: {brand} reads plain text log files and prints a short summary: how many lines there are, which levels they use and which messages repeat the most. It is one small binary with no dependencies.
features: Reads files, directories and standard input
Groups similar messages without any configuration
Prints text, JSON or a small HTML report
bundles.quick_out:
app.log: 48 211 lines, 3 levels
  info   46 902
  warn    1 190
  error     119
top message: cache miss for key (9 413 times)
bundles.install_intro: {brand} is distributed as a single binary. There is nothing to configure before the first run.
install_steps: Download the archive that matches your system.
Unpack it and copy the binary to a directory on your PATH.
Run the version command to check that it works.

usage.p: Point {brand} at a file, a directory or a pipe. Directories are read recursively and compressed files are unpacked on the fly.
usage.code:
{cmd} summary app.log
{cmd} summary /var/log/myapp/
cat app.log | {cmd} summary -

usage.p: Use --since and --until to narrow the summary to a time range. Times can be absolute or relative to now.
The default output is plain text. JSON is stable and meant for scripts; the HTML report is a single file you can send to a colleague.
usage.code:
{cmd} summary --format json app.log
{cmd} summary --format html app.log

options.d: Only lines after this time, absolute or such as 2h.
Only lines before this time.
Only lines of this level or above.
How many repeated messages to list. Default 5.
text, json or html. Default text.

faq.a: Anything line based. {brand} recognises common timestamp and level styles and falls back to plain lines when it does not.

faq.q: How big a file can it read?
faq.a: Files are streamed, so size is limited only by time. A gigabyte takes a few seconds on a laptop.

bundles.desc: {brand} turns a folder of Markdown files and a few templates into a static website.
bundles.overview: {brand} turns a folder of Markdown files and a few templates into a static website. There is no database, no runtime and nothing to keep up to date on the server.
features: A local preview that rebuilds on every save
bundles.quick_out: Serving notes at localhost:4000 (press Ctrl+C to stop)
bundles.install_intro: {brand} is a single executable. Put it on your PATH and you are done.
install_steps: Download the archive that matches your system.
Unpack it and copy the executable to a directory on your PATH.
Run the version command to check that it works.

usage.p: The init command creates a folder with a config file, a layout and one example page.
Pages are Markdown files. The front matter at the top sets the title and the date; everything below it is the content.
usage.code:
title: First note
date: 2025-03-14
---
Some words about the first note.

usage.p: The build command writes the finished site to the public folder. Copy that folder to any web server.

options.d: Folder for the finished site. Default public.
Include pages marked as drafts.
Port for the preview server. Default 4000.
Rebuild when a file changes.
Print errors only.

faq.q: Can I use my own templates?
faq.a: Yes. Templates are plain HTML files with a few placeholders, and the folder layout is yours to change.
No. The output is plain files that any web server can serve.

faq.q: How do I add a new kind of page?
faq.a: Add a folder under pages with its own layout file and {brand} will pick it up on the next build.

bundles.desc: {brand} runs small recurring jobs on one machine and tells you when one of them fails.
bundles.overview: {brand} runs small recurring jobs on one machine and tells you when one of them fails. It is a friendlier alternative to a crontab you have to keep in your head.
features: One line of output per job, so failures stand out
bundles.quick:
{cmd} add backup 'every day at 03:00' 'tar czf notes.tgz notes'
{cmd} list
bundles.quick_out: backup   every day at 03:00   last run: ok (4 s)
bundles.install_intro: {brand} is a single executable plus a small background process that checks the schedule once a minute.
install_steps: Download the archive that matches your system.
Unpack it and copy the executable to a directory on your PATH.
Start the background process with your system's service manager.

usage.p: A job has a name, a schedule and a command. Schedules are written in plain words.
usage.code:
{cmd} add backup 'every day at 03:00' 'tar czf notes.tgz notes'
{cmd} add tidy 'every monday' 'rm -r tmp/old'

usage.p: The list command shows every job with the result of its last run. The history command shows the runs of one job with their duration and output.
Pausing keeps the job and its history but stops it from running. Useful while you move house or restore a backup.

options.d: Where jobs and logs are kept. Default is a folder in your home.
Print only failures.
How many runs history shows. Default 10.
Machine readable output.
Run a job right away as well as on schedule.

faq.q: Does it need to run as a service?
faq.a: Yes, a small background process checks the schedule once a minute. The install page shows what to start.

faq.q: What happens if the computer is off?
faq.a: A job that was due while the machine was off runs once when it starts again.

faq.q: Can jobs depend on each other?
faq.a: Not yet. Chain the commands in a single job for now.

bundles.tagline: Select, sort and join CSV files
bundles.desc: {brand} selects, sorts, joins and cleans CSV files from the command line.
bundles.overview: {brand} selects, sorts, joins and cleans CSV files from the command line. It handles large files without loading them into memory and never changes the input.
features: Fix common problems such as stray quotes and mixed line endings
bundles.quick:
{cmd} select name,city people.csv
{cmd} sort --by city people.csv
bundles.install_intro: {brand} is a single executable with no dependencies.
install_steps: Download the archive that matches your system.
Unpack it and copy the executable to a directory on your PATH.
Run the version command to check that it works.

usage.p: The select command prints only the columns you name, in the order you give them. A column can be renamed with an equals sign.
usage.code:
{cmd} select name,city people.csv
{cmd} select id,town=city people.csv

usage.p: The filter command keeps the rows that match a simple condition. Several conditions can be combined.
The join command combines two files on a column they share. Rows without a match are dropped unless you ask for them.

options.d: Field separator. Default is a comma.
Set to false if the first row is data.
Write to a file instead of the screen.
Column to sort by.
Column to join on.

faq.q: How large a file can it handle?
faq.a: Files are processed as a stream, so memory use stays small. Sorting large files uses temporary space on disk.
No. Output goes to the screen or to a new file.
Use the delimiter option for tabs, semicolons or any single character.
